title: Σκύλλη καὶ Χάρυβδις
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus’s men row past the Sirens while he, bound, and with their ears stopped with wax, listens; once the song is out of hearing they free him. At once the ship meets smoke, a great wave and a crash; the frightened men let go of the oars, and Odysseus goes through the ship rousing them, tells the rowers to strike the surf, and orders the helmsman to keep clear of the smoke and wave and hold to the crag. He does not tell them of Scylla and, forgetting Circe’s warning against fighting her, puts on armour and watches from the prow. In the strait he describes Charybdis gulping and vomiting the sea; while the crew looks at her, Scylla snatches six of the strongest men from the ship, and he sees them eaten at her doors, the most pitiable sight of all his wanderings. Beyond the strait they reach the island of the Sun, where he hears the cattle and sheep, remembers the warnings of Teiresias and Circe, and tells his men to row past it; their hearts break, and Eurylochus answers him with hateful words.

sentences.t: ὣς φάσαν ἱεῖσαι ὄπα κάλλιμον·
sentences.tr: hōs phasan hieisai opa kallimon·
sentences.l: So they spoke, sending forth a fair voice;
sentences.i: So they spoke, sending out their fair voice;
sentences.n: The Sirens’ speech closed in the previous part, so this is Odysseus’s own narration again, and a new paragraph begins. ὣς φάσαν is ‘so they spoke’, φάσαν being ἔφασαν, the third plural of φημί without the augment. ἱεῖσαι is the feminine participle of ἵημι ‘send forth’, ὄπα is the accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’, and κάλλιμον ‘fair’ is built on κάλλος ‘beauty’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὸν κῆρ
ἤθελ’ ἀκουέμεναι, λῦσαί τ’ ἐκέλευον ἑταίρους
ὀφρύσι νευστάζων·
sentences.tr:
autar emon kēr
ēthel’ akouemenai, lysai t’ ekeleuon hetairous
ophrysi neustazōn·
sentences.i: but my heart wished to hear, and I bade my companions loose me, signalling with my brows;
sentences.n: Odysseus is bound and his men’s ears are stopped with wax (see 196 and 199–200), so he can only signal. ἐμὸν κῆρ is ‘my heart’, the subject of ἤθελ’ (ἤθελε, elided), and ἀκουέμεναι is the epic infinitive ‘to hear’ (Attic ἀκούειν). λῦσαι is the aorist infinitive ‘to loose’, with ‘me’ understood, and ἐκέλευον is ‘I bade’. νευστάζων is ‘nodding’ (a repeated nod), with ὀφρύσι ‘with my brows’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 194.

sentences.t: οἱ δὲ προπεσόντες ἔρεσσον.
sentences.tr: hoi de propesontes eresson.
sentences.l: And they, falling forward, rowed.
sentences.i: They threw themselves forward and rowed.
sentences.n: οἱ is the pronoun ‘they’, the men at the oars, and the article-form is a pronoun, as often in Homer. προπεσόντες is the aorist participle of προπίπτω ‘fall forward’, here ‘throwing themselves forward’ on the oars, and ἔρεσσον is the imperfect of ἐρέσσω ‘row’.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἀνστάντες Περιμήδης Εὐρύλοχός τε
πλείοσί μ’ ἐν δεσμοῖσι δέον μᾶλλόν τε πίεζον.
sentences.tr:
autika d’ anstantes Perimēdēs Eurylochos te
pleiosi m’ en desmoisi deon mallon te piezon.
sentences.l:
And at once, rising up, Perimedes and Eurylochus
with more bonds bound me, and pressed me the harder.
sentences.i: At once Perimedes and Eurylochus rose and bound me with more bonds, and pressed me tighter.
sentences.n: Perimedes and Eurylochus are two of Odysseus’s companions; Eurylochus is named again as the speaker in the last unit of this part. ἀνστάντες is ἀναστάντες ‘having risen’, and δέον is the unaugmented imperfect of δέω ‘bind’. πλείοσι is the dative plural ‘more’ with δεσμοῖσι ‘bonds’, and μᾶλλον ‘more’ goes with πίεζον, the imperfect of πιέζω ‘squeeze, press’; μ’ is ‘me’ and serves both verbs.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τάς γε παρήλασαν, οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔπειτα
φθογγῆς Σειρήνων ἠκούομεν οὐδέ τ’ ἀοιδῆς,
αἶψ’ ἀπὸ κηρὸν ἕλοντο ἐμοὶ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι,
ὅν σφιν ἐπ’ ὠσὶν ἄλειψ’, ἐμέ τ’ ἐκ δεσμῶν ἀνέλυσαν.
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē tas ge parēlasan, oud’ et’ epeita
phthongēs Seirēnōn ēkouomen oude t’ aoidēs,
aips’ apo kēron helonto emoi eriēres hetairoi,
hon sphin ep’ ōsin aleips’, eme t’ ek desmōn anelysan.
sentences.l:
But when they had sailed past them, and no longer after that
the voice of the Sirens did we hear, nor their song,
at once the wax took off my trusty companions,
which I had smeared on their ears, and from the bonds they loosed me.
sentences.i: But when they had rowed past the Sirens, and we no longer heard the voice or the song of the Sirens, my trusty companions at once took off the wax that I had smeared on their ears, and loosed me from the bonds.
sentences.n: The wax and the bonds come off once the Sirens are out of hearing. παρήλασαν is the aorist of παρελαύνω ‘drive past’, with τάς ‘them’, the Sirens, as object (the article is a pronoun). ἠκούομεν takes the genitives φθογγῆς ‘voice’ and ἀοιδῆς ‘song’, and οὐδέ τ’ is ‘nor’. ἀπὸ … ἕλοντο is tmesis, ‘took off’, and ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι is the stock phrase ‘trusty companions’; the exact sense of ἐρίηρος is not fully known. ἐμοί, ‘to me’, stands for ‘my’. ὅν is the relative ‘which’, σφιν is ‘for them’, ἄλειψ’ is ἄλειψα ‘I had smeared’ (aorist of ἀλείφω, elided), and ἀνέλυσαν is the aorist of ἀναλύω ‘loose’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὴν νῆσον ἐλείπομεν, αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα
καπνὸν καὶ μέγα κῦμα ἴδον καὶ δοῦπον ἄκουσα.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē tēn nēson eleipomen, autik’ epeita
kapnon kai mega kyma idon kai doupon akousa.
sentences.l:
But when indeed we were leaving the island, at once then
smoke and a great wave I saw, and a crash I heard.
sentences.i: But when we were leaving the island, I saw smoke and a great wave at once, and heard a crash.
sentences.n: Past the Sirens’ island the ship meets its next danger, here only smoke, a great wave and a crash; the strait itself is named at 234–236. τὴν νῆσον is ‘the island’, the Sirens’ (τήν is the ordinary definite article here), and ἐλείπομεν is the imperfect of λείπω ‘we were leaving’. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist ‘I saw’ (Attic εἶδον), and ἄκουσα is ἤκουσα ‘I heard’ without the augment. δοῦπον is ‘a heavy sound, a crash’. The poem does not say here what the smoke is; line 219 shows that it, with the wave, marks the place to steer clear of.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄρα δεισάντων ἐκ χειρῶν ἔπτατ’ ἐρετμά,
βόμβησαν δ’ ἄρα πάντα κατὰ ῥόον·
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ ara deisantōn ek cheirōn eptat’ eretma,
bombēsan d’ ara panta kata rhoon·
sentences.l:
And of them, afraid, out of their hands flew the oars,
and all things boomed along the current;
sentences.i: They were afraid, and the oars flew from their hands, and everything went booming down the current;
sentences.n: The men let go of the oars in fright. τῶν δ’ … δεισάντων is a genitive absolute, ‘they being afraid’, from δείδω ‘fear’. ἔπτατ’ is ἔπτατο, the aorist of πέτομαι ‘fly’, singular after the neuter plural ἐρετμά ‘oars’. βόμβησαν is the aorist of βομβέω ‘boom, hum’, and πάντα ‘all things’ is probably the oars, which the Greek does not say; κατὰ ῥόον is ‘down the current’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 204.

sentences.t:
ἔσχετο δ’ αὐτοῦ
νηῦς, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτ’ ἐρετμὰ προήκεα χερσὶν ἔπειγον.
sentences.tr:
escheto d’ autou
nēus, epei ouket’ eretma proēkea chersin epeigon.
sentences.l:
and stopped, right there,
the ship, since no longer the tapering oars with their hands they plied.
sentences.i: and the ship stopped where she was, since they no longer plied the tapering oars with their hands.
sentences.n: ἔσχετο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘was checked, stopped’, and αὐτοῦ is ‘on the spot’; νηῦς ‘ship’ stands at the start of the next line. ἐπεί is ‘since’. προήκεα is usually taken as ‘tapering’, an epithet of the oars, and ἔπειγον is the imperfect of ἐπείγω ‘press, ply’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ διὰ νηὸς ἰὼν ὤτρυνον ἑταίρους
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι παρασταδὸν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον·
sentences.tr:
autar egō dia nēos iōn ōtrynon hetairous
meilichiois epeessi parastadon andra hekaston·
sentences.l:
But I, going through the ship, urged on my companions
with gentle words, standing-beside each man:
sentences.i: But I went through the ship and urged on my companions with gentle words, standing beside each man:
sentences.n: A speech follows (208–221); the colon says so. ὤτρυνον is the imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and διὰ νηός is ‘through the ship’. The second line is the formula already met at 10.173: μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι is ‘with gentle words’, παρασταδόν ‘standing beside’, and ἄνδρα ἕκαστον ‘each man’.

sentences.t: ὦ φίλοι, οὐ γάρ πώ τι κακῶν ἀδαήμονές εἰμεν·
sentences.tr: ō philoi, ou gar pō ti kakōn adaēmones eimen·
sentences.l: “O friends, for we are not yet in any way unversed in evils;
sentences.i: “Friends, until now we have not been strangers to trouble;
sentences.n: Odysseus’s speech to the crew begins here and runs to 221; he argues from the Cyclops. ὦ φίλοι is ‘O friends’. ἀδαήμων ‘unversed’, from the root of δαῆναι ‘learn, know’, takes the genitive κακῶν ‘of evils’, and εἰμεν is the epic form of ἐσμέν ‘we are’. The γάρ gives the reason for what follows: they have come through worse.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν δὴ τόδε μεῖζον ἕπει κακόν, ἢ ὅτε Κύκλωψ
εἴλει ἐνὶ σπῆι γλαφυρῷ κρατερῆφι βίηφιν·
sentences.tr:
ou men dē tode meizon hepei kakon, ē hote Kyklōps
eilei eni spēi glaphyrōi kraterēphi biēphin·
sentences.l:
not indeed is this a greater evil that is upon us, than when the Cyclops
was shutting us in in the hollow cave by strong might;
sentences.i: This evil that now befalls us is surely no greater than when the Cyclops shut us in his hollow cave by his strong might;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν δή is ‘surely not’, and μεῖζον ‘greater’ goes with ἢ ὅτε ‘than when’. ἕπει is read as a form of ἕπω ‘be about, attend’, here ‘is upon us’; the form is unusual. εἴλει is the imperfect of εἴλω ‘shut in’, σπῆι the dative of σπέος ‘cave’ and γλαφυρῷ ‘hollow’. κρατερῆφι βίηφιν carries the ending -φι(ν), which marks the instrument: ‘by strong might’. ‘Us’ is understood after εἴλει.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔνθεν ἐμῇ ἀρετῇ, βουλῇ τε νόῳ τε,
ἐκφύγομεν, καί που τῶνδε μνήσεσθαι ὀίω.
sentences.tr:
alla kai enthen emēi aretēi, boulēi te noōi te,
ekphygomen, kai pou tōnde mnēsesthai oiō.
sentences.l:
but even from there by my excellence, and by counsel and by mind,
we escaped, and I think we shall perhaps be mindful of these things.
sentences.i: but even from there we escaped through my excellence, my counsel and my mind, and I think that perhaps we shall remember this too.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν is ‘from there’, that is from the Cyclops’s cave. Three datives give the means: ἀρετῇ ‘excellence’, here skill in a crisis rather than moral virtue, βουλῇ ‘counsel’ and νόῳ ‘mind’. ἐκφύγομεν is the unaugmented aorist ‘we escaped’. καί που … ὀίω is ‘and I think that perhaps …’, ὀίω being the first person of οἴομαι, and μνήσεσθαι is the future infinitive of μιμνήσκομαι ‘be mindful of’, taking the genitive τῶνδε ‘these things’: Odysseus predicts that the present danger too will become a memory.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἄγεθ’, ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω, πειθώμεθα πάντες.
sentences.tr: nyn d’ ageth’, hōs an egō eipō, peithōmetha pantes.
sentences.l: But now come, as I may say, let us all obey.
sentences.i: Now come, let us all obey in the way I shall tell you.
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ἄγεθ’ is ‘but now come’, ἄγεθ’ being the plural ἄγετε. ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω is ‘as I may say’, an indefinite clause with ἄν and the aorist subjunctive, and πειθώμεθα is the first plural subjunctive ‘let us obey’ (literally ‘let us be persuaded’), with πάντες ‘all’. The orders follow.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς μὲν κώπῃσιν ἁλὸς ῥηγμῖνα βαθεῖαν
τύπτετε κληίδεσσιν ἐφήμενοι, αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς
δώῃ τόνδε γ’ ὄλεθρον ὑπεκφυγέειν καὶ ἀλύξαι·
sentences.tr:
hymeis men kōpēisin halos rhēgmina batheian
typtete klēidessin ephēmenoi, ai ke pothi Zeus
dōēi tonde g’ olethron hypekphygeein kai alyxai·
sentences.i: As for you, strike the deep surf of the salt sea with your oars, sitting at the oarlocks, if Zeus may somehow grant that we flee from this destruction and escape it;
sentences.n: These are the orders to the rowers. ὑμεῖς μέν ‘you, on the one hand’ is answered by σοὶ δέ ‘and to you’ in the next unit. κώπῃσιν is the dative plural ‘with oars’, ῥηγμῖνα is ‘the surf, the breaking of the waves’ with βαθεῖαν ‘deep’, and ἁλός is ‘of the salt-sea’. κληίδεσσιν is the dative plural of κληΐς, a part of the rowing-gear: ‘rowing-bench’ is the house rendering in the literal layer and ‘oarlock’ in the other, and the exact object is not certain. αἴ κε is ‘if perhaps’, with δώῃ, the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι (Attic δῷ); this takes the infinitives ὑπεκφυγέειν (epic -έειν) and ἀλύξαι ‘to flee from and to escape’, with τόνδε ὄλεθρον ‘this destruction’.

sentences.t: σοὶ δέ, κυβερνῆθ’, ὧδ’ ἐπιτέλλομαι·
sentences.tr: soi de, kybernēth’, hōd’ epitellomai·
sentences.l: And to you, helmsman, thus I give charge:
sentences.i: And to you, helmsman, I give this charge:
sentences.n: Now the helmsman is addressed. κυβερνῆθ’ is the vocative κυβερνῆτα ‘helmsman’, elided, with the τ printed θ before the rough breathing of ὧδ’. ἐπιτέλλομαι is ‘I give charge’ and takes the dative σοί; ὧδε is ‘thus, as follows’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 217.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
βάλλευ, ἐπεὶ νηὸς γλαφυρῆς οἰήια νωμᾷς.
sentences.tr:
all’ eni thymōi
balleu, epei nēos glaphyrēs oiēia nōmāis.
sentences.l:
but in your heart
lay it, since of the hollow ship the steering-gear you handle.
sentences.i: Lay it in your heart, since you are the one who handles the steering-gear of the hollow ship.
sentences.n: ἐνὶ θυμῷ βάλλευ is ‘lay it in your heart’; βάλλευ is the middle imperative of βάλλω with the epic ending -ευ for -εο, ‘put for yourself’. ἐπεί is ‘since’, and νηὸς γλαφυρῆς is ‘of the hollow ship’. οἰήια is the plural of οἰήιον, the steering-gear, a steering-oar or rudder; the passage does not describe the fitting. νωμᾷς is the second singular of νωμάω ‘handle, ply’.

sentences.t:
τούτου μὲν καπνοῦ καὶ κύματος ἐκτὸς ἔεργε
νῆα, σὺ δὲ σκοπέλου ἐπιμαίεο, μή σε λάθῃσι
κεῖσ’ ἐξορμήσασα καὶ ἐς κακὸν ἄμμε βάλῃσθα.
sentences.tr:
toutou men kapnou kai kymatos ektos eerge
nēa, sy de skopelou epimaieo, mē se lathēisi
keis’ exormēsasa kai es kakon amme balēistha.
sentences.l:
From this smoke and wave outside keep
the ship, and you for the crag make, lest she escape your notice
darting off thither, and into evil us you cast.”
sentences.i: Keep the ship outside this smoke and wave, and make for the crag, in case she darts off that way unnoticed by you, and you cast us into evil.”
sentences.n: ἐκτός takes the genitive, ‘outside of’: τούτου μὲν καπνοῦ καὶ κύματος ἐκτὸς ἔεργε νῆα is ‘keep the ship outside this smoke and wave’, ἔεργε being the imperative of εἴργω ‘hold off’. The μέν is answered by σὺ δέ ‘and you’. ἐπιμαίεο is the imperative of ἐπιμαίομαι ‘make for, aim at’, with the genitive σκοπέλου ‘crag’. μή σε λάθῃσι is ‘lest she escape your notice’, the ship being the subject of λάθῃσι and of ἐξορμήσασα ‘having darted off’; κεῖσ’ is ‘thither’, presumably toward the smoke and wave. βάλῃσθα is the second singular aorist subjunctive active with the old ending -σθα (= βάλῃς), ‘you cast’, and ἄμμε is the epic ‘us’. The speech ends here, so the English closes the quotation.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, οἱ δ’ ὦκα ἐμοῖς ἐπέεσσι πίθοντο.
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hoi d’ ōka emois epeessi pithonto.
sentences.l: So I spoke, and they quickly to my words were persuaded.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and they quickly yielded to my words.
sentences.n: The speech is over and a new paragraph resumes the narrative; the same line stands at 10.178. ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’, ἐφάμην being the imperfect of φημί. πίθοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of πείθομαι ‘be persuaded, obey’, and ἐμοῖς ἐπέεσσι is ‘to my words’, with ὦκα ‘quickly’.

sentences.t:
Σκύλλην δ’ οὐκέτ’ ἐμυθεόμην, ἄπρηκτον ἀνίην,
μή πώς μοι δείσαντες ἀπολλήξειαν ἑταῖροι
εἰρεσίης, ἐντὸς δὲ πυκάζοιεν σφέας αὐτούς.
sentences.tr:
Skyllēn d’ ouket’ emytheomēn, aprēkton aniēn,
mē pōs moi deisantes apollēxeian hetairoi
eiresiēs, entos de pykazoien spheas autous.
sentences.l:
But Scylla no longer I mentioned, an un-doable distress,
lest somehow, taking fright, my companions would cease
from rowing, and pack themselves inside.
sentences.i: But I said no more of Scylla, a distress beyond remedy, in case my companions, frightened, should stop rowing and huddle together inside the ship.
sentences.n: Odysseus now says what he kept from the men: he does not go on to speak of Scylla. οὐκέτ’ ἐμυθεόμην is ‘I no longer spoke of’, from μυθέομαι ‘speak, tell’, with Σκύλλην as its object. ἄπρηκτον ἀνίην stands in apposition: ἄπρηκτος is ‘not to be done, that cannot be dealt with’ and ἀνίη ‘trouble, distress’. μή πώς … ἀπολλήξειαν is a negative purpose clause with the optative after a past tense, ‘lest somehow they should cease’, taking the genitive εἰρεσίης ‘from rowing’; πυκάζοιεν σφέας αὐτούς is ‘they would cover themselves closely’, that is huddle inside.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δὴ Κίρκης μὲν ἐφημοσύνης ἀλεγεινῆς
λανθανόμην, ἐπεὶ οὔ τί μ’ ἀνώγει θωρήσσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
kai tote dē Kirkēs men ephēmosynēs alegeinēs
lanthanomēn, epei ou ti m’ anōgei thōrēssesthai·
sentences.l:
And then indeed of Circe’s grievous behest
I forgot, since she was in no way bidding me to arm myself;
sentences.i: And then I forgot Circe’s grievous behest, since she was in no way bidding me to arm myself;
sentences.n: Earlier in Book 12 (12.116–126, especially 121–123) Circe warned Odysseus not to fight Scylla; here he says he forgot that behest. καὶ τότε δή is ‘and then indeed’. Κίρκης ἐφημοσύνης ἀλεγεινῆς are genitives after λανθανόμην, from λανθάνομαι ‘forget’; ἐφημοσύνη is ‘behest, instruction’, and ἀλεγεινῆς ‘grievous’. ἐπεὶ οὔ τί μ’ ἀνώγει θωρήσσεσθαι is ‘since she was in no way bidding me to arm myself’: ἀνώγει is the past of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, and θωρήσσεσθαι is ‘to arm oneself’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ καταδὺς κλυτὰ τεύχεα καὶ δύο δοῦρε
μάκρ’ ἐν χερσὶν ἑλὼν εἰς ἴκρια νηὸς ἔβαινον
πρῴρης·
sentences.tr:
autar egō katadys klyta teuchea kai dyo doure
makr’ en chersin helōn eis ikria nēos ebainon
prōirēs·
sentences.i: But I put on my famous armour, took two long spears in my hands, and stepped onto the decking at the ship’s prow;
sentences.n: Odysseus arms himself and goes to the bow to watch for Scylla. καταδύς is the aorist participle of καταδύω, ‘having gone down into’, here ‘putting on’, with the object κλυτὰ τεύχεα ‘famous armour’. δοῦρε is the dual of δόρυ ‘spear’, ‘two spears’, with μάκρ’ ‘long’ and ἑλών ‘having taken’. ἴκρια are the planks of a deck or platform, rendered ‘decking’, and νηὸς … πρῴρης is ‘of the ship, of the prow’. ἔβαινον is the imperfect of βαίνω ‘step’. The unit ends at the ano teleia after πρῴρης, which opens line 230.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν γάρ μιν ἐδέγμην πρῶτα φανεῖσθαι
Σκύλλην πετραίην, ἥ μοι φέρε πῆμ’ ἑτάροισιν.
sentences.tr:
enthen gar min edegmēn prōta phaneisthai
Skyllēn petraiēn, hē moi phere pēm’ hetaroisin.
sentences.l:
for from there I expected her first to appear,
Scylla of the rock, who to me brought woe on my companions.
sentences.i: for from there I expected her to appear first, Scylla of the rock, who to my cost brought woe on my companions.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν γάρ is ‘for from there’, from the prow. μιν is ‘her’, the pronoun standing before the name Σκύλλην in the next line. ἐδέγμην is a past tense of δέχομαι ‘await, expect’, taking the future infinitive φανεῖσθαι ‘to appear’, with πρῶτα ‘first’. πετραίην is ‘of the rock’, from πέτρα. ἥ μοι φέρε πῆμ’ ἑτάροισιν is ‘who brought woe on my companions’: φέρε is the unaugmented imperfect of φέρω, πῆμα is ‘woe’, and μοι is a dative of interest, ‘to my cost’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ πῃ ἀθρῆσαι δυνάμην, ἔκαμον δέ μοι ὄσσε
πάντῃ παπταίνοντι πρὸς ἠεροειδέα πέτρην.
sentences.tr:
oude pēi athrēsai dynamēn, ekamon de moi osse
pantēi paptainonti pros ēeroeidea petrēn.
sentences.l:
And nowhere could I catch sight of her, and wearied for me my eyes
as I peered everywhere toward the misty-looking rock.
sentences.i: But I could not see her anywhere, and my eyes grew weary as I peered in every direction toward the misty-looking rock.
sentences.n: οὐδέ πῃ is ‘nor anywhere’, and ἀθρῆσαι is the aorist infinitive ‘to catch sight of’, with ‘her’ understood. ἔκαμον is the aorist of κάμνω ‘grow weary’, with the dual ὄσσε ‘eyes’ as subject and μοι ‘my’. The participle παπταίνοντι agrees with μοι, ‘as I peered’, and πάντῃ is ‘in every direction’. ἠεροειδέα is the stock epithet ‘misty-looking’, built on ἀήρ ‘mist’.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς μὲν στεινωπὸν ἀνεπλέομεν γοόωντες·
sentences.tr: hēmeis men steinōpon anepleomen gooōntes·
sentences.l: We, on the one hand, the narrow passage sailed up, groaning;
sentences.i: We sailed up the narrows, groaning aloud;
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the ship enters the strait. στεινωπόν is the Ionic spelling of στενωπόν ‘a narrow place, strait’ (the object of ἀνεπλέομεν, ‘sailed up’ it). ἀνεπλέομεν is the imperfect of ἀναπλέω ‘sail up’, and γοόωντες is the uncontracted participle of γοάω ‘groan, wail’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν μὲν Σκύλλη, ἑτέρωθι δὲ δῖα Χάρυβδις
δεινὸν ἀνερροίβδησε θαλάσσης ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
enthen men Skyllē, heterōthi de dia Charybdis
deinon anerroibdēse thalassēs halmyron hydōr.
sentences.l:
on one side Scylla, and on the other heavenly Charybdis
dreadfully sucked down the sea’s salt water.
sentences.i: On one side lay Scylla, and on the other heavenly Charybdis dreadfully sucked down the salt water of the sea.
sentences.n: These lines name the two sides of the strait. ἔνθεν μέν … ἑτέρωθι δέ is ‘on this side … on the other’; the verb ἀνερροίβδησε belongs to Charybdis, and Scylla has none until ἕλεθ’ in line 246. δῖα Χάρυβδις keeps the stock epithet ‘heavenly’ although it sits oddly on a monster. ἀνερροίβδησε is the aorist of ἀναρροιβδέω ‘suck down’, a verb for the rush of the down-draught. δεινόν is a neuter accusative used as an adverb, ‘dreadfully’, and ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ is ‘salt water’.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὅτ’ ἐξεμέσειε, λέβης ὣς ἐν πυρὶ πολλῷ
πᾶσ’ ἀναμορμύρεσκε κυκωμένη, ὑψόσε δ’ ἄχνη
ἄκροισι σκοπέλοισιν ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔπιπτεν·
sentences.tr:
ē toi hot’ exemeseie, lebēs hōs en pyri pollōi
pas’ anamormyreske kykōmenē, hypsose d’ achnē
akroisi skopeloisin ep’ amphoteroisin epipten·
sentences.i: Whenever she vomited it out, all of her would seethe up with a roar, churned like a cauldron on a great fire, and the spray would fall high on the tops of both crags;
sentences.n: What follows is Charybdis’s cycle, told as repeated action, so the English says ‘whenever … would’: ὅτ’ ἐξεμέσειε uses the optative, the aorist optative of ἐξεμέω ‘vomit out’, and ἀναμορμύρεσκε is the iterative (-σκε) of ἀναμορμύρω ‘seethe up with a roar’. ἦ τοι is ‘truly’, λέβης ὣς ἐν πυρὶ πολλῷ is ‘like a cauldron on a great fire’, and κυκωμένη is ‘churned’. ἄχνη is ‘spray’ and ὑψόσε ‘on high’; ἄκροισι σκοπέλοισιν is ‘on the tops of the crags’, with ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ‘on both’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτ’ ἀναβρόξειε θαλάσσης ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ,
πᾶσ’ ἔντοσθε φάνεσκε κυκωμένη, ἀμφὶ δὲ πέτρη
δεινὸν ἐβεβρύχει, ὑπένερθε δὲ γαῖα φάνεσκε
ψάμμῳ κυανέη·
sentences.tr:
all’ hot’ anabroxeie thalassēs halmyron hydōr,
pas’ entosthe phaneske kykōmenē, amphi de petrē
deinon ebebrychei, hypenerthe de gaia phaneske
psammōi kyaneē·
sentences.l:
But whenever she gulped back the sea’s salt water,
all of her inside would appear churned, and around, the rock
dreadfully would roar, and below the earth would appear
dark with sand;
sentences.i: But whenever she gulped the salt water of the sea back down, all of her would appear churned up within, and around her the rock would roar dreadfully, and below the ground would show dark with sand;
sentences.n: The other half of the cycle: the gulping down. ἀναβρόξειε is the aorist optative of ἀναβρόχω ‘gulp back down’, ἔντοσθε is ‘within’, and φάνεσκε is the iterative of φαίνομαι ‘would appear’. ἀμφί is ‘around’, and ἐβεβρύχει is a reduplicated past form of βρύχω ‘roar’, probably a pluperfect used like an imperfect, here ‘would roar’. ὑπένερθε is ‘below’, γαῖα ‘earth, the sea-floor’, ψάμμῳ ‘with sand’ (dative) and κυανέη ‘dark’, built on the same κυανο- ‘dark’ as in κυανόπρῳρος. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 243.

sentences.t: τοὺς δὲ χλωρὸν δέος ᾕρει.
sentences.tr: tous de chlōron deos hēirei.
sentences.l: and them pale fear was seizing.
sentences.i: and pale fear seized them.
sentences.n: τοὺς is the pronoun ‘them’, the crew. χλωρὸν δέος is ‘pale fear’, χλωρός being the pallid, greenish colour of a frightened face, and ᾕρει is the imperfect of αἱρέω with its augment, ‘was seizing’.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς μὲν πρὸς τὴν ἴδομεν δείσαντες ὄλεθρον·
sentences.tr: hēmeis men pros tēn idomen deisantes olethron·
sentences.l: We toward her looked, fearing destruction;
sentences.i: We looked toward her, in fear of destruction;
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’, Charybdis (the article is a pronoun), and ἴδομεν is the unaugmented aorist ‘we looked’ (Attic εἴδομεν). δείσαντες is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’, with ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’ as its object. The μέν is answered by τόφρα δέ ‘but meanwhile’ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δέ μοι Σκύλλη γλαφυρῆς ἐκ νηὸς ἑταίρους
ἓξ ἕλεθ’, οἳ χερσίν τε βίηφί τε φέρτατοι ἦσαν.
sentences.tr:
tophra de moi Skyllē glaphyrēs ek nēos hetairous
hex heleth’, hoi chersin te biēphi te phertatoi ēsan.
sentences.l:
but meanwhile to me Scylla from the hollow ship my companions
six took, who in hands and in might were the best.
sentences.i: But meanwhile Scylla took six of my companions out of the hollow ship, the ones who were best in hands and in might.
sentences.n: τόφρα is ‘meanwhile’. ἕλεθ’ is ἕλετο, the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘took’, elided; ἓξ is ‘six’, with ἑταίρους as object, and the dative μοι is ‘from me, to my loss’. οἳ … φέρτατοι ἦσαν is ‘who were the best’, with χερσίν ‘in hands’ and βίηφι ‘in might’, the ending -φι marking respect or instrument.

sentences.t:
σκεψάμενος δ’ ἐς νῆα θοὴν ἅμα καὶ μεθ’ ἑταίρους
ἤδη τῶν ἐνόησα πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν
ὑψόσ’ ἀειρομένων·
sentences.tr:
skepsamenos d’ es nēa thoēn hama kai meth’ hetairous
ēdē tōn enoēsa podas kai cheiras hyperthen
hypsos’ aeiromenōn·
sentences.i: Looking toward the swift ship and, at the same time, among my companions, I already saw their feet and hands lifted high above;
sentences.n: σκεψάμενος is the aorist participle of σκέπτομαι ‘look’, with ἐς νῆα θοήν ‘to the swift ship’ and μεθ’ ἑταίρους ‘among my companions’. ἤδη is ‘already’, and ἐνόησα is ‘I perceived’, with the accusatives πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ‘feet and hands’ and τῶν ‘of them’, which goes with πόδας καὶ χεῖρας and is agreed with by the participle ἀειρομένων ‘as they were lifted’, the passive of ἀείρω. ὕπερθεν is ‘from above, overhead’ and ὑψόσ’ ‘on high’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 249.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δὲ φθέγγοντο καλεῦντες
ἐξονομακλήδην, τότε γ’ ὕστατον, ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ.
sentences.tr:
eme de phthengonto kaleuntes
exonomaklēdēn, tote g’ hystaton, achnymenoi kēr.
sentences.l:
and me they cried out, calling
by-name, then for the last time, grieving in heart.
sentences.i: and they cried out to me, calling me by name, then for the last time, grieving in heart.
sentences.n: φθέγγοντο is the imperfect middle of φθέγγομαι ‘cry out’, and καλεῦντες is the epic form of the participle of καλέω ‘call’ (= καλέοντες, Attic καλοῦντες). ἐξονομακλήδην is ‘by name’, an adverb built on ὄνομα ‘name’ and the root of καλέω; τότε γ’ ὕστατον is ‘then for the last time’. ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ is ‘grieving in heart’, κῆρ ‘heart’ being an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἐπὶ προβόλῳ ἁλιεὺς περιμήκεϊ ῥάβδῳ
ἰχθύσι τοῖς ὀλίγοισι δόλον κατὰ εἴδατα βάλλων
ἐς πόντον προΐησι βοὸς κέρας ἀγραύλοιο,
ἀσπαίροντα δ’ ἔπειτα λαβὼν ἔρριψε θύραζε,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ epi probolōi halieus perimēkeï rhabdōi
ichthysi tois oligoisi dolon kata eidata ballōn
es ponton proïēsi boos keras agrauloio,
aspaironta d’ epeita labōn erripse thyraze,
sentences.l:
And as when on a jutting point a fisherman with a very long rod
for the little fishes a trick, among baits, casting,
into the open-sea lets down the horn of a field-dwelling ox,
and the gasping one then taking flings it outside,
sentences.i: And as when a fisherman on a jutting point, with a very long rod, casting a lure among baits for the little fish, lets the horn of a field-dwelling ox down into the sea, and then takes the gasping catch and flings it outside,
sentences.n: A simile: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ‘and as when’ opens it, and ὣς in the next unit brings it back to the men. προβόλῳ is ‘a jutting point’, περιμήκεϊ ‘very long’, and ῥάβδῳ ‘rod’. δόλον κατὰ εἴδατα βάλλων is ‘casting a trick among baits’: δόλος is the lure, and κατά with εἴδατα ‘foods’ is taken as ‘among morsels’, though the exact construction is not certain. ἐς πόντον προΐησι is ‘lets down into the open sea’, and βοὸς κέρας ἀγραύλοιο is ‘the horn of a field-dwelling ox’; the Greek says only that the horn is lowered, not what it does. ἀσπαίροντα is ‘gasping, struggling’, and θύραζε is ‘out of doors, outside’. Here the unit is cut at the comma, since the whole simile would run past four lines.

sentences.t: ὣς οἵ γ’ ἀσπαίροντες ἀείροντο προτὶ πέτρας·
sentences.tr: hōs hoi g’ aspairontes aeironto proti petras·
sentences.l: so they, gasping, were lifted toward the rocks;
sentences.i: so they, gasping, were lifted up toward the rocks;
sentences.n: ὣς οἵ γ’ is ‘so they’, returning from the simile to the men. ἀσπαίροντες is the same verb as ἀσπαίροντα in the simile, ‘gasping’, and ἀείροντο is the imperfect passive of ἀείρω ‘were lifted’. προτί is πρός ‘toward’, and πέτρας ‘rocks’ is the accusative plural.

sentences.t:
αὐτοῦ δ’ εἰνὶ θύρῃσι κατήσθιε κεκληγῶτας
χεῖρας ἐμοὶ ὀρέγοντας ἐν αἰνῇ δηιοτῆτι·
sentences.tr:
autou d’ eini thyrēisi katēsthie keklēgōtas
cheiras emoi oregontas en ainēi dēiotēti·
sentences.l:
And right there at her doors she devoured them, as they screamed,
stretching out their hands to me in fearsome fighting;
sentences.i: And right there at her doors she devoured them as they screamed, stretching out their hands to me in fearsome fighting;
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’, and εἰνὶ θύρῃσι is ‘at the doors’, εἰνί being ἐνί; the doors are those of Scylla’s lair, which the passage does not otherwise describe. κατήσθιε is the imperfect of κατεσθίω ‘devour’, and κεκληγῶτας is the perfect participle of κλάζω ‘shriek’, agreeing with the men. ὀρέγοντας is ‘stretching out’, from ὀρέγω, with χεῖρας ‘hands’ and ἐμοί ‘to me’. δηιοτῆτι is the dative of δηιοτής ‘fighting, battle’, and αἰνῇ is ‘fearsome’, from αἰνός.

sentences.t:
οἴκτιστον δὴ κεῖνο ἐμοῖς ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι
πάντων, ὅσσ’ ἐμόγησα πόρους ἁλὸς ἐξερεείνων.
sentences.tr:
oiktiston dē keino emois idon ophthalmoisi
pantōn, hoss’ emogēsa porous halos exereeinōn.
sentences.l:
Most pitiable indeed that with my own eyes I saw
of all that I toiled through, searching out the paths of the salt-sea.
sentences.i: That was the most pitiable sight my own eyes saw of all that I toiled through in searching out the paths of the salt sea.
sentences.n: Odysseus judges what he has just seen. οἴκτιστον is the superlative of οἰκτρός ‘pitiable’, δή ‘indeed’, and κεῖνο ‘that’ (Attic ἐκεῖνο). ἐμοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖσι is ‘with my own eyes’, in the dative in -οισι, and ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist ‘I saw’. πάντων ὅσσ’ ἐμόγησα is ‘of all that I toiled through’, from μογέω ‘toil’, and πόρους ἁλός is ‘the paths of the salt-sea’, with ἐξερεείνων ‘searching out’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πέτρας φύγομεν δεινήν τε Χάρυβδιν
Σκύλλην τ’, αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα θεοῦ ἐς ἀμύμονα νῆσον
ἱκόμεθ’·
sentences.tr:
autar epei petras phygomen deinēn te Charybdin
Skyllēn t’, autik’ epeita theou es amymona nēson
hikometh’·
sentences.i: But when we had escaped the rocks, and dread Charybdis, and Scylla, then at once we came to the blameless island of the god;
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the strait is behind them and they reach the next island. πέτρας φύγομεν δεινήν τε Χάρυβδιν Σκύλλην τ’ is ‘we fled the rocks and dread Charybdis and Scylla’, with φύγομεν the unaugmented aorist and δεινήν ‘dread’; αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα is ‘at once then’. The god is the Sun, named in the next unit. ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is the stock epithet; its meaning is not actually known, ‘blameless’ being only the traditional gloss. ἱκόμεθ’ is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘arrive’, and the unit ends at the ano teleia in line 262.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔσαν καλαὶ βόες εὐρυμέτωποι,
πολλὰ δὲ ἴφια μῆλ’ Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο.
sentences.tr:
entha d’ esan kalai boes eurymetōpoi,
polla de iphia mēl’ Hyperionos Ēelioio.
sentences.l:
And there were fine cattle, broad-browed,
and many stout flocks of the Sun Hyperion.
sentences.i: There were fine cattle, broad of brow, and many stout flocks belonging to the Sun, Hyperion.
sentences.n: This is the island of the Sun, Thrinacia, which Circe described earlier in Book 12. ἔσαν is the epic ἦσαν ‘there were’, καλαί is ‘fine’, βόες ‘cattle’ and εὐρυμέτωποι ‘broad-browed’; ἴφια μῆλα is ‘stout flocks’, μῆλα being the small livestock, sheep and goats. Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο is ‘of the Sun Hyperion’, Hyperion being a name or epithet of the Sun; elsewhere he is Ὑπεριονίδης ‘son of Hyperion’ (12.176).

sentences.t:
δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἔτι πόντῳ ἐὼν ἐν νηὶ μελαίνῃ
μυκηθμοῦ τ’ ἤκουσα βοῶν αὐλιζομενάων
οἰῶν τε βληχήν·
sentences.tr:
dē tot’ egōn eti pontōi eōn en nēi melainēi
mykēthmou t’ ēkousa boōn aulizomenaōn
oiōn te blēchēn·
sentences.i: Then, while I was still on the open sea in the black ship, I heard the lowing of cattle settling in for the night and the bleating of sheep;
sentences.n: Odysseus hears the herds from the sea. δὴ τότ’ is ‘then indeed’, ἐών is the epic participle ‘being’ (Attic ὤν), and πόντῳ is ‘on the open-sea’. ἐν νηὶ μελαίνῃ is ‘in the black ship’. ἤκουσα takes the genitive μυκηθμοῦ ‘lowing’ and the accusative βληχήν ‘bleating’, both possible with this verb. αὐλιζομενάων, with the epic genitive ending -άων, is ‘lodging in the yard, spending the night’, and οἰῶν is the genitive plural of ὄις ‘sheep’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 266.

sentences.t:
καί μοι ἔπος ἔμπεσε θυμῷ
μάντηος ἀλαοῦ, Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο,
Κίρκης τ’ Αἰαίης, ἥ μοι μάλα πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλε
νῆσον ἀλεύασθαι τερψιμβρότου Ἠελίοιο.
sentences.tr:
kai moi epos empese thymōi
mantēos alaou, Thēbaiou Teiresiao,
Kirkēs t’ Aiaiēs, hē moi mala poll’ epetelle
nēson aleuasthai terpsimbrotou Ēelioio.
sentences.l:
and into my heart fell the word
of the blind seer, Theban Teiresias,
and of Aeaean Circe, who very much laid charge on me
to avoid the island of the mortal-delighting Sun.
sentences.i: and into my heart fell the word of the blind seer, Theban Teiresias, and of Circe of Aeaea, who charged me most earnestly to avoid the island of the Sun, who delights mortals.
sentences.n: The word that comes to mind is a warning: Teiresias’s and Circe’s, given earlier in the tale, about this island. ἔπος ἔμπεσε θυμῷ is ‘a word fell into my heart’, ἔμπεσε being the unaugmented aorist of ἐμπίπτω. μάντηος ἀλαοῦ is ‘of the blind seer’, μάντηος being the epic genitive of μάντις (Attic μάντεως), and Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο ‘of Theban Teiresias’ with the epic genitive -αο. Κίρκης τ’ Αἰαίης is ‘and of Aeaean Circe’; ἥ is the relative ‘who’, ἐπέτελλε ‘charged’, and μάλα πόλλ’ ‘very much’. ἀλεύασθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’. τερψιμβρότου, ‘mortal-delighting’, is built on τέρπω ‘delight’ and βροτός ‘mortal’, like φαεσίμβροτος ‘mortal-lighting’ of the same god at 10.138. Line 267 (μάντηος ἀλαοῦ, Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο) is metrically irregular as transmitted: the final short syllable of μάντηος has to be counted long at the start of the second foot, before ἀλαοῦ.

sentences.t: δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἑτάροισι μετηύδων ἀχνύμενος κῆρ·
sentences.tr: dē tot’ egōn hetaroisi metēudōn achnymenos kēr·
sentences.l: Then indeed I among my companions spoke, grieving in heart:
sentences.i: Then, grieving in heart, I spoke among my companions:
sentences.n: The line is the one that opened his earlier speech to the crew at 12.153; another speech to them follows (271–276). δὴ τότ’ is ‘then indeed’. μετηύδων is the first-person imperfect of μεταυδάω ‘speak among’, with ἑτάροισι ‘my companions’, and ἀχνύμενος κῆρ is ‘grieving in heart’, κῆρ being an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ μύθων κακά περ πάσχοντες ἑταῖροι,
ὄφρ’ ὑμῖν εἴπω μαντήια Τειρεσίαο
Κίρκης τ’ Αἰαίης, ἥ μοι μάλα πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλε
νῆσον ἀλεύασθαι τερψιμβρότου Ἠελίοιο·
sentences.tr:
keklyte meu mythōn kaka per paschontes hetairoi,
ophr’ hymin eipō mantēia Teiresiao
Kirkēs t’ Aiaiēs, hē moi mala poll’ epetelle
nēson aleuasthai terpsimbrotou Ēelioio·
sentences.l:
“Hear my words, evils though suffering, companions,
so that I may tell you the oracles of Teiresias
and of Aeaean Circe, who very much laid charge on me
to avoid the island of the mortal-delighting Sun;
sentences.i: “Hear my words, companions, suffering woes as you are, so that I may tell you the oracles of Teiresias and of Circe of Aeaea, who charged me most earnestly to avoid the island of the Sun, who delights mortals;
sentences.n: Odysseus now tells the crew the warning he has been keeping in mind. The first line also stands at 10.189, there with a comma after μύθων. κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, and μευ is the genitive ‘my’ with μύθων ‘words’. κακά περ πάσχοντες is ‘though suffering evils’, περ giving the concession, and ἑταῖροι is the vocative ‘companions’. ὄφρ’ ὑμῖν εἴπω is ‘so that I may tell you’, with the aorist subjunctive, and μαντήια, ‘oracles’, are the utterances of a seer, from μάντις. Lines 273–274 repeat 268–269 word for word, and so does the English.

sentences.t: ἔνθα γὰρ αἰνότατον κακὸν ἔμμεναι ἄμμιν ἔφασκεν.
sentences.tr: entha gar ainotaton kakon emmenai ammin ephasken.
sentences.l: for there the most fearsome evil to be for us she kept saying.
sentences.i: for she kept saying that the most fearsome evil would be there for us.
sentences.n: ἔνθα γάρ is ‘for there’, on the island. αἰνότατον is the superlative of αἰνός ‘fearsome’, and κακόν ‘evil’ is the subject of ἔμμεναι, the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι), after ἔφασκεν ‘she kept saying’, an iterative imperfect of φημί. ἄμμιν is the epic ‘to us’ (Attic ἡμῖν).

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ παρὲξ τὴν νῆσον ἐλαύνετε νῆα μέλαιναν.
sentences.tr: alla parex tēn nēson elaunete nēa melainan.
sentences.l: But beyond the island drive the ship, the black one.”
sentences.i: So drive the black ship on past the island.”
sentences.n: The order that follows from the warning. ἀλλά is ‘but’, here ‘so’, and παρέξ is ‘past, beyond’, taking the accusative τὴν νῆσον. ἐλαύνετε is the present imperative of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, said of the ship and its rowers, and νῆα μέλαιναν is ‘the black ship’. The speech ends here, so the English closes the quotation.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, τοῖσιν δὲ κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, toisin de kateklasthē philon ētor.
sentences.l: So I spoke, and in them was broken their dear heart.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and their dear hearts were broken within them.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the men’s answer to the order. The line also stands at 10.198, where it runs on; here it ends at a full stop. τοῖσιν is the epic dative ‘in them’, and φίλον ἦτορ is ‘dear heart’, the singular standing for the heart of each man. κατεκλάσθη is the aorist passive of κατακλάω ‘break down’.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ Εὐρύλοχος στυγερῷ μ’ ἠμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: autika d’ Eurylochos stygerōi m’ ēmeibeto mythōi·
sentences.l: And at once Eurylochus answered me with a hateful word:
sentences.i: At once Eurylochus answered me in hateful words:
sentences.n: Eurylochus is the companion who helped bind Odysseus at 195; the colon announces his speech, which comes in the next part. αὐτίκα δ’ is ‘and at once’. στυγερῷ μύθῳ is ‘with a hateful word’, στυγερός being ‘hateful’, and ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, with μ’ ‘me’.
